Getting Your Green Laning Gear Right

Good green laning gear is not about looking the part; it is about staying safe, comfortable and mobile when you are miles from the nearest road on a rough byway. The demands of laning sit somewhere between road touring and off-road enduro, which means the kit you already own for tarmac work is rarely ideal. Over years of riding lanes in all weathers on everything from a Benelli TRK 502 to bigger adventure machinery, I have learned what earns its place in the shed and what does not. This guide runs through the essentials, in rough order of importance, so a beginner can build a sensible kit without wasting money. If you are new to the activity, pair this with our green laning beginner's guide first.

Boots: Your Most Important Purchase

If you buy one piece of dedicated laning kit, make it boots. Your feet and ankles are horribly exposed the moment you dab, paddle through a rut or drop the bike, and a road touring boot offers little protection against a twisting fall or a rock strike. A proper adventure or enduro boot has a rigid shin plate, ankle bracing and a sole designed to grip pegs and mud.

For serious off-road bias, the Alpinestars Tech 7 Enduro Boots offer near-motocross levels of protection while still being walkable, which matters when you are opening gates or scouting a line on foot. If you want something that also works for the road ride to the lanes and back, the Forma Adventure Boots are a superb all-rounder: waterproof, comfortable for walking and protective enough for most laning. For a fuller breakdown read our dedicated guide to adventure motorcycle boots.

Helmet and Goggles

An adventure-style helmet with a peak and a large eyeport transforms laning. The peak shades low sun and deflects roost, while the roomy aperture lets you wear goggles, which seal far better than a visor against dust and rain when you are moving slowly and sweating hard. The Arai Tour-X5 Helmet is a benchmark adventure lid with excellent ventilation and the option to run either a visor or goggles. Pair it with a set of 100% Barstow Goggles for the rougher, slower sections where you want maximum airflow and a proper seal. Our adventure helmets review compares the leading options in detail.

Green laning is hot, physical work at low speed. Ventilation is not a luxury; overheating and fogging cause more incidents on the lanes than the terrain does. Choose kit that breathes.

Armoured, Vented Riding Kit

The ideal laning suit is a vented adventure jacket and trouser combination with removable, certified armour at the shoulders, elbows, hips and knees, plus a back protector. Laning involves constant low-speed effort, so you generate a lot of heat, and a heavily insulated touring suit will cook you. Look for large air vents, a removable thermal liner for cold days and a separate waterproof layer rather than a bulky all-in-one. Good armour matters more here than abrasion resistance, because most laning offs are low-speed tumbles onto hard ground. If your jacket's back protector is a token foam pad, upgrade it, and read our guides to motorcycle back protectors and knee armour to make sure the impact protection is genuinely up to the job.

Gloves

Laning gloves need to balance protection, feel and weather resistance. You want enough dexterity to work the clutch precisely and enough armour to save your hands in a fall. A pair of adventure gloves such as the Klim Adventure GTX Gloves gives waterproofing and knuckle protection for mixed days. Many experienced laners carry a second, lighter enduro glove for hot, dry technical sections where feel matters most. If you ride year round, our guide to waterproof motorcycle gloves covers the winter end of the spectrum.

Tyres: Knobbly Versus 50/50

Nothing changes a laning bike's character like tyres, and the choice comes down to how you split your miles. If you ride mostly tarmac to reach the lanes and only dabble off road, a 50/50 dual-sport tyre such as the Continental TKC80 Tyres gives a fine compromise, with genuine bite in the dirt and acceptable road manners and life. If your priority is grip on soft, wet and rocky lanes and you accept shorter road life and more noise, a more aggressive tyre like the Motoz Tractionator Adventure Tyre transforms confidence when the going gets serious. Whichever you fit, dropping tyre pressures a little for the off-road sections dramatically improves grip; just remember to reinflate for the road. Our adventure tyre guide goes deeper into the trade-offs.

Luggage, Hydration and Tools

Laning luggage should be soft, tough and mounted low and secure. Hard panniers are a liability off road, catching on ruts and bending mounts in a fall. A rugged soft pack such as the Kriega OS-18 Adventure Pack straps securely and shrugs off knocks. Carry water where you can reach it, ideally in a hydration pack, because laning is thirsty work and you will not always pass a shop.

A tool and puncture kit is non-negotiable. A flat tyre miles down a byway is a walk home without one.

  • A tyre puncture repair kit suited to your wheels, plus a means of reinflating such as a compact 12V compressor or CO2 canisters.
  • Tyre levers and, for tubed wheels, a spare tube.
  • A basic tool roll with the sizes your bike needs, plus zip ties and strong tape.
  • A tow strap, a compact first aid kit and a foil survival blanket.

Communication and Navigation

A Bluetooth intercom lets a group stay in contact and warn each other of hazards without stopping every hundred yards, and it doubles as your link to turn-by-turn navigation. Speaking of which, a rugged GPS or a well-mounted phone running offline maps is essential, since phone signal vanishes on the very lanes where you most need to confirm you are on a legal right of way. Always carry a paper OS map and compass as a backup; batteries die at the worst moments. For remote solo riding, many laners now carry a satellite messenger for genuine emergencies.

Building Your Kit Sensibly

You do not need everything at once. Prioritise boots, then a decent helmet and gloves, then armour, then tyres and luggage as your ambitions grow. Buy the protective kit new and to a proper standard, and save your money on the accessories. With the right gear you will ride further, safer and with far more enjoyment. When you are kitted out, put it to use with our guides to the best green lanes in the UK and the Trans Euro Trail UK section.
